> **Experimental.** The multivariate extension of `ridge()` is new in genridge 0.8.1. Its
> functions, arguments and results may change in future versions. This article is a
> **draft**, shown on the package website but not included in the package.

## Introduction

When there are several response variables, $\mathbf{Y}$ ($n \times q$), to be predicted from
the same set of collinear predictors, $\mathbf{X}$ ($n \times p$), the multivariate linear
model (MLM) $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{E}$ suffers from collinearity in the
same way as a univariate regression. The simplest multivariate ridge estimator uses one
ridge constant, $\lambda$, for all responses [@BreimanFriedman:1997, eq. 6.3]:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{B}}(\lambda) = (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{Y} \enspace .
$$

Because the penalty involves only $\mathbf{X}$, each column of $\widehat{\mathbf{B}}(\lambda)$
is exactly the univariate ridge estimate for that response. What the multivariate view adds is:

* a **common** choice of $\lambda$, using criteria pooled over the responses;
* the **covariance of the coefficients across responses**. For predictor $j$, its
  coefficients for all $q$ responses (row $j$ of $\widehat{\mathbf{B}}$) have covariance
  matrix $[\mathbf{V}_\lambda]_{jj}\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, where
  $\mathbf{V}_\lambda = (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X} (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X} + \lambda \mathbf{I})^{-1}$
  depends only on the predictors and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is the residual covariance matrix
  of the responses. That is,
  $\text{Var}(\text{vec}\, \widehat{\mathbf{B}}) = \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \otimes \mathbf{V}_\lambda$.

genridge fits these models with `ridge()`, given a matrix response, and provides plots of both
kinds: within one response, as for univariate ridge regression [@Friendly:genridge:2013], and
across responses.

## Example: school data

The `schooldata` data set in the **heplots** package comes from an evaluation of Program
Follow Through [@Charnes-etal-1981]. For 70 schools, three measures of student achievement,
`reading`, `mathematics` and `selfesteem`, are to be predicted from five measures of the
schools' resources: `education` and `occupation` (of the parents), `visit` (parental visits to
the school), `counseling` (parent counseling) and `teacher` (number of teachers).

```{r schooldata}
data(schooldata, package = "heplots")
str(schooldata)
```

Three of the predictors are almost the same variable, so the collinearity is severe:

```{r school-collinearity}
round(cor(schooldata[, c("education", "occupation", "visit", "counseling", "teacher")]), 2)
school.mlm <- lm(cbind(reading, mathematics, selfesteem) ~
                   education + occupation + visit + counseling + teacher, data = schooldata)
car::vif(lm(reading ~ education + occupation + visit + counseling + teacher, data = schooldata))
```

As a result, some OLS coefficients have the "wrong" sign. `visit` is strongly and positively
correlated with reading and mathematics, but its coefficients for these are negative, while
those for `occupation` are inflated:

```{r school-ols}
coef(school.mlm)
```

### Fitting

`ridge()` with a matrix response (here, `cbind()` in the model formula) fits all responses with
the same ridge constants and returns an object of class `"mlmridge"`. As the criteria below
show, the optimal values of $\lambda$ are small for these data, so the grid of ridge constants
is fine at the low end.

```{r school-ridge}
lambda <- c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 5)
sridge <- ridge(cbind(reading, mathematics, selfesteem) ~
                  education + occupation + visit + counseling + teacher,
                data = schooldata, lambda = lambda)
sridge
```

The HKB, LW and GCV criteria are calculated for each response. GCV is also pooled over
responses (by default, scaling each response by its residual variance, so the result does not
depend on the units of the responses) to give a common value:

```{r school-criteria}
sridge$criteria
sridge$kGCV.pooled
```

### Trace plots

`traceplot()` shows the univariate ridge trace plot for each response, one panel each:

```{r school-traceplot}
#| fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%",
#| fig.cap = "Ridge trace plots for the three responses in the school data."
traceplot(sridge)
```

All three responses show the same pattern: `occupation`'s large coefficient shrinks quickly,
and `visit`'s negative coefficients for reading and mathematics become positive, but only at
$\lambda \approx 1$ (reading) and $\lambda \approx 2$ (mathematics), well past the values
suggested by the criteria. This is an important
lesson: the amount of shrinkage that is best for _prediction_ (which the criteria aim for) may
be much less than is needed to make the coefficients _interpretable_.

### Within one response

`as.ridge()` extracts the results for one response as an ordinary `"ridge"` object, and the
plot methods accept `response =` to do this directly. The bivariate ridge trace plot for
`occupation` and `visit`, for reading, shows the path of the two coefficients and their
covariance ellipses:

```{r school-plot}
#| fig.cap = "Bivariate ridge trace plot for occupation and visit, for reading."
plot(sridge, response = "reading", variables = c("occupation", "visit"),
     radius = 0.5, fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1)
```

### Across responses

With `predictor =`, `plot()` shows instead the coefficients of one predictor for **two
responses**, with their covariance ellipses, across $\lambda$. Because the covariance matrix of
a predictor's coefficients is $[\mathbf{V}_\lambda]_{jj}\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, all the ellipses
have the same shape and orientation, that of the residual covariance of the two responses;
only their size and center change.

```{r school-cross}
#| fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4, out.width = "100%",
#| fig.cap = "Coefficients for reading and mathematics, with covariance ellipses, for three predictors."
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (p in c("occupation", "visit", "counseling"))
  plot(sridge, predictor = p, responses = c("reading", "mathematics"), fill = TRUE)
par(op)
```

These show things a univariate view cannot:

* `visit`'s coefficients cross zero for **both** responses together, as $\lambda$ increases.
* `counseling`'s coefficients move _away_ from the origin. Ridge regression shrinks the length
  of the whole vector of coefficients, not each one: with highly correlated predictors, some
  coefficients grow while others shrink.

The ellipses are long and thin, because the residuals for reading and mathematics are highly
correlated:

```{r school-sigma}
round(cov2cor(sridge$Sigma), 3)
```

Note that these ellipses show the sampling variability of a _biased_ estimate; unlike the
confidence ellipses of `heplots::coefplot()`, whether they cover the origin is not a test.

### Other summaries

Since all responses share the same predictors and ridge constants, the variance inflation
factors are the same for every response:

```{r school-vif}
vif(sridge)
```

## Simulation: bias and variance with known coefficients

With real data, we cannot see how close the estimates are to the true coefficients. A
simulation, in which the true $\mathbf{B}$ is known, shows the tradeoff of bias and variance
directly. We use the six (very collinear) predictors from Longley's data, and generate three
responses with known coefficients and correlated errors.

genridge centers the predictors and scales them to unit mean square, so we define the true
coefficients on that scale:

```{r sim-setup}
X <- data.matrix(longley[, c("GNP", "Unemployed", "Armed.Forces",
                             "Population", "Year", "GNP.deflator")])
n <- nrow(X)
Xs <- scale(X, scale = FALSE)
Xs <- Xs / rep(sqrt(colMeans(Xs^2)), each = n)

B <- 4 * cbind(Y1 = c( 1.0, -1.0,  0.5, 0.0, 1.0,  0.5),
               Y2 = c( 0.5,  0.5,  0.5, 0.5, 0.5,  0.5),
               Y3 = c( 1.5,  0.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.0, -1.0))
rownames(B) <- colnames(X)
Sigma <- matrix(0.5, 3, 3); diag(Sigma) <- 1      # error covariance: correlation 0.5
```

We simulate 1000 data sets, fit a multivariate ridge regression to each, and record the
estimates and the value of $\lambda$ chosen by pooled GCV.

```{r sim-run}
lambda <- c(0, 0.002, 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10)
nsim <- 1000
set.seed(1234)
L <- chol(Sigma)
est <- array(NA, c(nsim, length(lambda), nrow(B), ncol(B)))
kGCV <- numeric(nsim)
for (r in 1:nsim) {
  Y <- Xs %*% B + matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n, 3) %*% L
  fit <- ridge(Y, X, lambda = lambda)
  est[r, , , ] <- coef(fit, type = "array")
  kGCV[r] <- fit$kGCV.pooled
}
```

The mean squared error of $\widehat{\mathbf{B}}(\lambda)$, summed over all coefficients,
splits into squared bias and variance:

```{r sim-mse}
Bbar <- apply(est, c(2, 3, 4), mean)
bias2 <- sapply(seq_along(lambda), function(i) sum((Bbar[i, , ] - B)^2))
variance <- sapply(seq_along(lambda), function(i) sum(apply(est[, i, , ], c(2, 3), var)))
mse <- data.frame(lambda, df = fit$df, bias2, variance, MSE = bias2 + variance)
mse
```

```{r sim-plot}
#| fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, out.width = "80%",
#| fig.cap = "Squared bias, variance and mean squared error of the ridge estimates against the effective degrees of freedom, over 1000 simulated data sets. The rug shows the values of df chosen by pooled GCV."
with(mse, {
  matplot(df, cbind(bias2, variance, MSE), type = "b", log = "y", pch = 15:17, lty = 1,
          col = c("blue", "red", "black"), lwd = 2,
          xlab = "Effective degrees of freedom", ylab = "Squared error (log scale)")
  legend("topleft", c("bias^2", "variance", "MSE"), col = c("blue", "red", "black"),
         pch = 15:17, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
  best <- which.min(MSE)
  abline(v = df[best], lty = 2)
})
rug(jitter(fit$df[match(kGCV, lambda)], amount = 0.03))
```

The variance of the OLS estimates ($\text{df} = 6$) is enormous, and even a little shrinkage
reduces it dramatically, at the cost of a small increase in bias. The MSE is smallest at
$\lambda = `r mse$lambda[which.min(mse$MSE)]`$ (df $\approx$
`r round(mse$df[which.min(mse$MSE)], 1)`), where it is about
`r round(mse$MSE[1] / min(mse$MSE))` times smaller than for OLS. The values of $\lambda$ chosen
by pooled GCV (median `r median(kGCV)`) are close to this optimum.

## Further directions

This extension is experimental. Planned or possible developments include:

* a display of all predictors' coefficient paths across two responses, to show how ridge
  regression pulls the coefficients of near-duplicate predictors together (the "grouping
  effect");
* **ridge HE plots**: hypothesis-error (HE) plots, as in the **heplots** package, showing how
  the hypothesis and error matrices change with $\lambda$;
* multivariate ridge estimators that shrink differently for each response, or across responses,
  such as that of @Brown-Zidek-1980.
